source_text: Cum igitur id a nobis abunde constet effectum; tamen quia operi nostro nascitur longitudo, sapiens lector intellegat, nobis quidem optabilem fuisse brevitatem, sed exegisse causae necessitatem, ut error saeculi favore diffusior, latiore veritatis acie vinceretur. Haud igitur de nihilo est, quod sermo noster extenditur. Adiutu enim Christi praesumo confore, ut nulla pars impietatis, contra quam nobis certamen est, aut negligenter quaesita, aut minus inventa, aut attrita mediocriter censeatur. Nec illud ergo desperare vel possumus, vel debemus, quoniam processu temporum tempestas excitata considat, et auctoritate sapientum vulgus ignavum quod nunc perstrepit corrigatur; sed voti quam sententiae minor causa est; quemvis enim status rerum exitum sortiatur, constabit nobis ratio et benignitatis et fidei. Neque enim pendemus ad prosperitatis popularis eventum. Scitum est siquidem illud trium in Babylone puerorum, qui cum a rege superbissimo ad adorandam statuam cogerentur, fidelissime restiterunt, neque anhela sunt fornace conterriti, quae accensa erat in religiosorum voratum; responderuntque ut et fidei et constantiae congruebat: Potens est, inquiunt, Deus, o rex, liberare nos de fornace hac; sed etiamsi non liberet, scito quoniam deos tuos non colimus, nec statuam quam erexisti adoramus [n11] . Quam sanctum votum iudicio miscuerunt, nec tamen consilii gravitatem desiderio levarunt! Fortitudinem fidei nec desperatione praecipitant, nec cupiditate suspendunt; miscent quidem vota; ceterum ordinem non relinquunt; consolantur tolerantiam h, sed iustis mitiora submittunt: Certum est, inquiunt, quoniam nos possit liberare Deus noster; sed utrum velit, est incertum; et ideo sub ambiguo rerum eventu stat piorum certa sententia, idola respuendi, supplicia perferendi. Viderit quid boni nostra liberatio etiam ceteris conferat; nobis interim veram felicitatem fides, inquiunt, invicta custodiat; non habet ergo mollioribus gratificandi nimiam necessitatem, cuius gloriae negotiantur adversa. De hac et nos disciplina, quam reliquerunt illustres magistri, intellegimus tenendam in prosperis votorum mediocritatem, in dogmatibus vero fidei consiliorum perennitatem; optamusque, persecutionum tumore compresso, etiam populis subvenire; at si id non accidat, stat quidquid acerbum est in contumeliis et periculis perpeti, quam non aversari illuviem sordesque manichaeas.
pass_a_gloss: Since therefore it stands abundantly accomplished by us; nevertheless because length is born for our work, let the wise reader understand that brevity was indeed desirable for us, but the necessity of the cause demanded that an error of the age more diffuse by favor be conquered by a broader battle-line of truth. Not therefore from nothing is it that our speech is extended. For with the help of Christ I presume it will come about that no part of the impiety against which our contest is may be judged either negligently sought, or less found, or worn down moderately. Nor therefore can we, or ought we, despair of this, that by the progress of times the storm stirred may settle, and by the authority of the wise the cowardly crowd which now makes a noise may be corrected; but the cause of the wish is less than of the sentence; for whatever end the status of things may receive, the reason both of kindness and of faith will stand for us. For we do not hang upon the event of popular prosperity. Known indeed is that of the three boys in Babylon, who when they were being compelled by a most proud king to adore a statue, most faithfully resisted, nor were they terrified by the panting furnace which had been kindled for the devouring of the religious; and they replied as suited both faith and constancy: God is able, they say, O king, to free us from this furnace; but even if he does not free, know that we do not worship your gods, nor do we adore the statue which you have erected. How holy a wish they mixed with judgment, nor nevertheless did they lighten the gravity of counsel by desire! They neither precipitate the fortitude of faith by desperation, nor hang it by desire; they mix wishes indeed; for the rest they do not leave the order; they console endurance, but they submit milder things to the just: It is certain, they say, that our God can free us; but whether he wills is uncertain; and therefore under an ambiguous event of things the certain sentence of the pious stands, of spitting out idols, of enduring punishments. Let it see what good our liberation confers even on the rest; for us meanwhile let unconquered faith, they say, guard true happiness; he therefore does not have an excessive necessity of gratifying the softer, whose adversities trade for glory. From this discipline also, which illustrious teachers left, we understand that a moderation of wishes is to be held in prosperous things, but in the dogmas of faith a perpetuity of counsels; and we wish, the swelling of persecutions having been compressed, to help even the peoples; but if that does not happen, it stands to endure whatever is bitter in insults and dangers rather than not to turn from Manichaean filth and dirt.

pass_b_english: Although it is established that we have achieved this abundantly, our work nevertheless grows long. Let the wise reader understand that brevity was indeed desirable to us, but the needs of the case demanded that error spread more widely by the world’s favor be defeated by a broader battle line of truth. Our discourse therefore extends for a reason. With Christ’s help, I trust that no part of the impiety against which we contend will be judged carelessly investigated, insufficiently discovered, or only moderately battered. We therefore neither can nor should despair that, as time advances, the storm that has arisen may subside and the authority of the wise correct the cowardly crowd now making its uproar. But our wish matters less than our settled judgment. Whatever outcome the state of affairs receives, our grounds of goodwill and faith will stand. We do not depend on the outcome of popular success. We know the declaration of the three young men in Babylon. When a most arrogant king tried to compel them to worship a statue, they resisted with complete faithfulness, undeterred by the panting furnace lit to devour the devout. They answered as faith and steadfastness required: ‘Our God is able, O king, to free us from this furnace. But even if he does not free us, know that we do not worship your gods or adore the statue you have set up’ (Daniel 3:17–18). How reverently they mingled desire with judgment, without letting desire weaken the weight of their resolve! They neither cast faith’s courage down through despair nor suspend it on craving. They include their wishes, but do not abandon the proper order; they comfort endurance, but subordinate gentler outcomes to just ones. ‘It is certain,’ they say, ‘that our God can free us; whether he wills to do so is uncertain. Therefore, amid the uncertain outcome of events, the devout hold to a certain resolution: to reject idols and endure punishments. Let God consider what good our deliverance may bring to others. Meanwhile,’ they say, ‘let undefeated faith preserve our true happiness.’ One whose adversity trades for his glory has no excessive need to indulge easier outcomes. From this discipline left by illustrious teachers, we too understand that we must maintain moderation in our wishes for prosperity, but permanence in our decisions about the doctrines of faith. We desire, with the swelling of persecution restrained, to help the peoples too. But if that does not happen, our resolution stands: to endure every bitterness of insult and danger rather than fail to reject Manichaean filth and pollution.
